cards.title: 1.1 History
body: The term history is derived from a Greek word historia, meaning inquiry.
History is thus broadly defined as the study of past developments.
The field of study that deals with these events is called History.
History is also defined as a record of the past.
To create this record, historians use sources such as documents, artifacts and artworks.

cards.title: 1.2 Pre-history
body: The period before writing was developed is known as the prehistoric period.
Archaeology is the study of past societies through an analysis of what people have left behind.

cards.title: 1.3 Sources of History
body: Historians rely on written records to write history of the past.
A source is the material out of which history is written.
In contrast, secondary sources are accounts of a particular period in history written later by someone who did not experience firsthand or participate in the events.
For example, Aynfelale, a history book of the 1940s that is written by the renowned Eritrean author and historian Alemseged Tesfai, is a secondary source of the 1940s.
The coin is the best example of a material source.

cards.title: 1.4 Dating Time in History
body: History can’t be written or can’t be known without the knowledge of the time when events occurred.
Actual dating method provides exact dates.
Relative dating method refers to measurement of time in terms of a decade, century and millennium.
A calendar is a system of measuring and recording time.
The Gregorian calendar is the most widely used calendar throughout the world.

cards.title: 1.5 Cause and Effect
body: Radiocarbon and Potassium-Argon dating methods are the two most often used dating methods.
In short, the history of society is the history of change.
A cause is something that makes an event or an action happen or exist.
An effect is the result or outcome of an action or an event.
Historians use cause and effect analyses to find the reason for what happened in the past.

cards.title: History
body: **Simple:** a true story of the past, checked with evidence.
**Formal:** the disciplined study of past human events using sources, dating, cause-and-effect and chronology.
**Analogy:** a court case — witnesses (sources), a timeline, and a verdict (interpretation), not a rumour.
**Example:** “Aksum traded ivory through Adulis” is history if inscriptions and archaeology back it.
**Non-example:** “My village is the oldest in the world because my uncle said so” — no source test.
**Misconception:** history = memorising dates. Dates are hooks; causes are the subject.
**Exam:** “Explain the importance of sources” → primary vs secondary + one limit of each.

cards.title: Chronology
body: **Prehistory** = before writing. We use tools, bones, paintings, carbon dates. **Primary source** = from the time (tablet, ruin, letter). **Secondary** = later account (your textbook). **BC/BCE** counts down to year 1; **AD/CE** counts up. Decade 10, century 100, millennium 1000. Cause → effect; many causes, not one villain. Chronology = the order — mix it up and the story lies.

cards.title: SPICE the past
body: Sources, Periods, Interpretation, Causes, Effects. Primary = “I was there.” Secondary = “I read about it.”

cards.title: More notes
body: A source is never simply true or false. Ask who made it, for whom, why, and what they could not know. A victory stele skips the king’s own dead. A tax list skips religion. Cross two types — a ruin plus a later chronicle — before you trust a number.

Time words: circa means about. A century is named for the hundred it is moving toward (1901–2000 is the 20th). BCE dates get smaller as you near year 1. When a question says “turn of the century,” name which century.

Cause essays: split long-term (geography, institutions) from a trigger (war, flood, murder). Effect essays: immediate vs later. Chronology mistakes are cheap ways to lose compare marks — jot a four-point timeline in the margin first.

glossary.meaning: History is a social necessity, i.e. no society can get along without knowledge of its history.

tips.text: History is the scientific study of past human developments, activities and events. It is so significant that no society can get along without knowledge of its history.
A society without history cannot have a proper sense of its own identity.
Historians classify all of human history into historic and prehistoric periods.
Historic period refers to the period after the beginning of writing; prehistoric period refers to the period before the beginning of writing.
Sources are the stuff out of which history is written.
Broadly speaking, sources are classified into two categories: primary and secondary.
The former is a source that came into existence during the actual period of the past that the historian is studying; the latter is an account written by historians studying a period in the past.
Moreover, sources can have different forms such as written, material and oral.
The ordering of time or chronology is basic to any study of the past.
Events must be examined in relation to those that preceded and followed them. However, in order to do this, historians need to establish dates of past events and developments.

lessons.title: Human Evolution and the Paleolithic Age

cards.title: 2.1 Human Evolution and the Paleolithic Age
body: Identify and describe the three stages of human evolution.
According to the scientific theory of evolution, the earliest humanlike creatures known as australopithecines lived in Africa as long as three to four million years ago.
A second stage in early human evolution occurred with the appearance of Homo erectus (“upright human being”) around 1.5 million years ago.
Homo erectus had relatively bigger brains and used stone tools.
Since hunting large animals required organization and communication, they formed small social organizations.

cards.title: Human Evolution and the Paleolithic Age
body: Paleolithic: tools of stone, fire, language, art, mobile bands. Evolution here is the long physical and cultural change toward Homo sapiens (use the book’s stage names). Civilisation features: cities, writing, specialised jobs, organised religion and rule, monuments, trade.

lessons.title: The Agricultural (Neolithic) Revolution and the Rise of Civilizations

cards.title: 2.2 The Agricultural (Neolithic) Revolution and the Rise of Civilizations
body: List the differences between the Paleolithic and Neolithic Ages.
The Neolithic Age is thus a period in human history extending from 8000 to 4000 B.C.E.
The Neolithic Revolution is, therefore, a revolution that occurred in the Neolithic Age.
The word Neolithic is Greek for “new stone”.
The name New Stone Age is, however, misleading.

cards.title: Neolithic revolution
body: **Simple:** people started farming and staying put.
**Formal:** the shift from foraging to food production, with domestication, surplus and settled villages — the platform for cities.
**Analogy:** switching from shopping daily with no fridge to growing a store-room.
**Example:** wheat and barley in Southwest Asia; later other crops elsewhere.
**Non-example:** a hunter who camps two nights is not yet Neolithic.
**Misconception:** farming was instantly easier. Early farming could mean more work and disease — it won by surplus and numbers.
**Exam:** link surplus → specialists → writing / government / inequality.

cards.title: FARMS → CITIES
body: Food surplus, Artisans, Rules, Monuments, Script. Paleolithic = old stone; Neolithic = new stone + farming.

cards.title: More notes
body: Paleolithic bands were not “waiting to become us.” They managed fire, season, and kinship with skill. What changes in the Neolithic is the store-room: grain and herds that can be counted, stolen, taxed and inherited. That store-room is why walls, priests and inequality show up together.

Civilisation is a bundle, not a medal. A society can have cities without an alphabet (early Andes later) or writing without huge cities. Use the book’s checklist, then admit extras. Farming began in more than one hearth — Southwest Asia is the exam’s first example, not the only one on Earth.
When you write “rise of civilisation,” name a river or rich coast, a staple crop, a form of record, and a ruler or temple. Four nouns beat a vague paragraph about “progress.”

cards.title: 2.3 Emergence of Civilizations
body: Generally speaking, culture is a people’s way of life.

The development of crop production and animal husbandry, the establishment of permanent settlements, and the subsequent expansion of trade and growth of towns and cities during the Neolithic age become the bases for the emergence of civilizations.
All the river valleys civilizations developed religions to explain the workings of nature such as the sun, rain, flood, life, and death.
As part of the religious beliefs of these civilizations, rulers claimed to possess divine power.
Eventually, all of the first civilizations used writing as a means of creative expression as well as for record keeping.

tips.text: According to archaeological and biological evidences, the earliest humanlike creatures (hominids) known as australopithecines lived in Africa as long as three to four million years ago.
The appearance of the australopithecines is considered as the first stage in human evolution.
A second stage in human evolution occurred with the appearance of Homo erectus in around 1.5 million years ago.
The third and most important stage in human evolution began with the emergence of Homo sapiens in around 250,000 years ago.
Homo sapiens gave rise to two distinct subgroups; Neanderthals and Homo sapiens sapiens.
Depending on the tools humans used, we generally classify human history from 2.5 million to 1200 B.C.E. into three ages. These are the Paleolithic, Neolithic and Bronze Ages.
In the Paleolithic Age, humans depended on hunting and gathering and used simple stone tools.
Eventually, hunting and gathering was replaced by agriculture with the introduction of systematic agriculture in the Neolithic Age. Also, humans used more refined stone tools in the Neolithic Age.
Following the Neolithic Age, starting from 3000 B.C.E., human beings began to use bronze extensively. Thus, the period that extends from 3000 to 1200 B.C.E is called the Bronze Age.
From all the three ages, the most important was the Neolithic.

units.title: Southwest Asia and Egypt (3500- 500 B.C.E)
units.intro: **Mesopotamia** (“between rivers” Tigris–Euphrates): Sumer city-states, cuneiform, ziggurat, unpredictable floods → irrigation + law (later Hammurabi). **Egypt**: Nile predictable flood, pharaoh as god-king, hieroglyphs, pyramids, afterlife bureaucracy. **Nubia**: south of Egypt, gold, kerma / later Kush, two-way influence. **Phoenicia**: cedar and purple, alphabet, sea trade. **Assyria** then **Persia**: big land empires, roads, satraps, tolerance mix.

cards.title: 3.1 Mesopotamian Civilization
body: Impact of Geography on Mesopotamian Civilization The Tigris and Euphrates Rivers are found in present day Iraq.

The ancient Greeks called the valley between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers Mesopotamia, meaning the land “between the rivers.” Mesopotamia was located at the eastern end of an area known as the Fertile Crescent.
The Fertile Crescent is an area of land that stretches from the Mediterranean Sea to the Persian Gulf.
Mesopotamia received little rain, but its soil had been enriched by layers of silt deposited by the two rivers.
Often, the Tigris and Euphrates overflowed their banks and deposited their fertile silt.

cards.title: 3.2 Egyptian Civilization
body: The Nile is a unique river, beginning in the highlands of Ethiopia and countries of the Great Lakes region (Burundi, Tanzania, Rwanda, and Uganda) and flowing northward to the Mediterranean Sea for more than 6346 kms.
Before it empties into the Mediterranean Sea, the Nile splits into two major branches.
The Nile Delta is called Lower Egypt; and the land to the south of the Nile Delta is called Upper Egypt.
Ancient Egypt’s important cities developed at the tip of the Nile Delta.
From ancient times, the Nile was considered the source of life in Egypt.

cards.title: 3.3 Nubian Civilization
body: Nubia lay south of Egypt between the first cataract of the Nile and the confluence of the blue and white Nile.
Unlike Egypt, Nubia had significant rainfall.
Nubia suitable for agriculture, trade and manufacturing.
As far as the period of the Old Kingdom, Nubia had trade relationship with Egypt.
The trade between the two regions increased after the first Nubian kingdom, known as Kerma, emerged in 2000 B.C.E.

cards.title: 3.4 Phoenician Civilization
body: Phoenicians were, therefore, a Semitic speaking people who lived along this narrow strip of land.
Phoenicia was not a unified state but a group of city-states, one of which usually dominated the others.
The most important Phoenician cities were Byblos, Sidon, Tyre and Beirut (all found in present day Lebanon).
The Phoenicians later set up a number of colonies such as the famous city of Carthage, found in present day Tunisia, in the western Mediterranean Sea.
The geographical location of Phoenicia played a big role in shaping the Phoenicians’ way of life.

cards.title: Nile = clock. Tigris = surprise.
body: Predictable flood → unified Egypt. Wild rivers → competing city-states. Alphabet gift = Phoenicians. Empire toolkit = Assyria/Persia.

cards.title: More notes
body: Sumer’s city-states fought over water and land; kingship is often a war-and-temple job. Writing begins as accountancy. Hammurabi is one late, famous freeze-frame of law, not the first or only code. Read a clause as social history: different penalties for different ranks tell you the hierarchy.

Egypt’s unity is a river highway plus a desert wall that made invasion rarer than in open Mesopotamia. Old, Middle and New Kingdoms (if your pages name them) are recoveries after collapse — the Nile does not abolish politics. Pyramids belong mainly to an early peak of royal display; later kings use hidden tombs.

Nubia is a partner and rival, not a footnote. Phoenicia shows that a thin coastal strip can punch above its size with ships and an easy script. Assyria and Persia scale up: provinces, roads, fear and, in Persia, a measured tolerance that kept taxes flowing.

tips.text: Between 3500 and 500 B.C.E., impressive civilizations and empires emerged in southwest Asia and Egypt.

The peoples of Mesopotamia and Egypt were the first to build civilizations. They developed marvelous cities and organized states. They developed writing systems that helped them to keep records and produce literature.
Also, they constructed monumental buildings in honor of their gods, to symbolize their power and to preserve their culture for posterity.
Mesopotamian and Egyptian societies were generally divided into three or four social classes.
Usually the royal families, the nobility, and the priests formed the upper class.
Below them stood merchants, artisans and lower government officials.
Below the class of merchants, artisans, and lower government officials were the majority of the peasants.

tips.text: Like the civilizations we have seen so far, geography influenced Indian and Chinese civilizations.

Also, the natural barriers surrounding them protected these civilizations from external invaders and limited their contacts with other societies.
Between 3000 and 1500 B.C.E., a flourishing civilization emerged in the valleys of the Indus River. This civilization is called Indus Valley or Harappan civilization.
The people who founded the Indus Valley civilization were a dark-skinned people known as Dravidians.
The two most important cities of the Indus valley civilization were Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro.
Over the course of time, the Indus valley civilization began to decline.
In about 1500 B.C.E., it was invaded by a group of IndoEuropean nomadic peoples from central Asia named Aryans.
The Aryan invasion brought about the final collapse of the Indus valley civilization and created a new Indian society based on their culture and institutions.
The Aryans introduced a new writing system known as Sanskrit. They also introduced Hinduism and a new social structure based on rigid caste divisions.

units.title: Greco-Roman Civilization
units.intro: **Greece:** mountains + sea → city-states (polis). Athens: experiment in citizen politics (limited — no women, slaves, foreigners). Sparta: military commune. Persian Wars then Athenian power; philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle); Alexander spreads a Greek mix (Hellenistic). **Rome:** republic (Senate, consuls, conflict of orders) → empire after civil wars. cards.title: 5.1 Greek Civilization
body: Geography played an important role in the development of Greek civilization.
Compared to the landmass of Mesopotamia and Egypt, Greece had a small area.
The mountains and the sea played significant roles in the development of Greek history.

The mountainous terrain had the effect of isolating the Greeks from one another.

body: Classical Greece (500338 B.C.E) Classical Greece is the name given to the period of Greek history from around 500 B.C.E. to the conquest of Greece by the Macedonian king Philip II in 338 B.C.E.

cards.title: More notes
body: A Greek citizen was a political animal in a small box. Colonies spread the box around the Mediterranean. After the Persian Wars, Athens builds a league that starts to look like an empire — which is why other Greeks fight the Peloponnesian War. Philosophy grows in that argumentative city: what is justice if the assembly can err?

Alexander dies young; the map does not snap back. Hellenistic kings run Greek-style cities over older peoples. Rome then swallows that world from the west. The republic’s genius is mixed government; its disease is successful generals with private armies. Augustus keeps republican furniture and changes who sits in it.

For essays: law and roads are how a peasant in Gaul becomes tied to a grain ship from Egypt. Slavery and conquest paid for the marble. End with a limit sentence so you do not sound like a tourist brochure.

tips.text: The most important were the last three periods.
During the Archaic period, Greece began to recover from the setbacks it faced during the dark age.
Two major developments stand out in the Archaic period: the emergence of the polis, or city-states, and the Greek’s colonization of the Mediterranean and Black Seas.
Following the Archaic age, Greek history entered into a period of remarkable intellectual and cultural growth known as the Classical period.
The Classical period, however, began with the war between the Greek states and the Persian Empire. In this war, the Greek citystates defeated the invading Persian army.
Forty years after the defeat of Persia, Greeks were divided among themselves, and eventually Sparta and Athens entered into a war known as the Peloponnesian war.

The next seventy years of Greek history, after the end of the Peloponnesian war, were marked by continuing warfare among the Greeks. As a result, Greek states entered a period of decline from 402 to 338 B.C.E.
While the Greek states were at war, Macedonia, a state north of mainland Greece, emerged as a strong state and occupied mainland Greece.
After this period, Greek history entered a new phase called the Hellenistic period.
The Hellenistic period was marked by the expansion of Greek language and culture throughout the Middle East and beyond.

units.title: Ancient and Medieval Eritrea
units.intro: People of this land mixed through the highland, the coast and the western lowlands over a long time — languages and livelihoods differ by belt. Ancient: South Arabian links, then the world of **Adulis** (port) and the highland state often named with **Aksum** — ivory, gold, incense, coins, stone monuments, Christian conversion in late antiquity. Medieval centuries: Islamic Red Sea connections, highland Christian polities, trade corridors, local chiefs — not an empty wait for Italy (that is Grade 10 Unit 12).

cards.title: 6.1 Origin of the Eritrean People
body: As part of the East African Great Rift Valley, in which most of the evidences for human origin have been discovered, Eritrean history is as old as humanity.
The recent discovery of a one million year old hominid cranium in Buya, northern Danakil Depression, testifies to this fact.
For thousands of years Eritrea had been inhabited by huntergatherer communities.
Generally speaking, present Eritrean society is the result of the interaction and integration of the pre-existing societies with waves of new incoming communities in different periods.
The first wave of migration was that of the Nilotic speaking group.

cards.title: 6.2 Ancient Eritrean Civilization
body: List the pre-Aksumite kingdoms and societies.
The earliest recorded history of Eritrea is found in the temples of ancient Egypt.
Starting from the Old Kingdom, Egyptians made trade expeditions to the Land of Punt, in present day Eritrea.
Pictures in Egyptian temples such as the funerary temple at Deir el-Bahri show maritime commerce between pharaohs of Egypt and local chiefs of the Red Sea coast of Eritrea.
Archaeological remains in the highlands and coastal areas of Eritrea suggest the presence of ancient civilizations and states long before the emergence of Aksum.

cards.title: More notes
body: Treat “origin of the Eritrean people” as a process: movements across the Red Sea, down the Nile corridor, and along the highland. Languages today still map some of those layers. Do not flatten farmers and pastoralists into one costume.

Ancient prosperity is a corridor story. Inland ivory and gold meet ships that already know Egypt, Arabia and India. Coins and inscriptions are how a highland court speaks to that wider room. Conversion to Christianity is a court event first; countryside follow-through takes time. Mosques and Islamic law on the coast later are the other door of the same sea.

Medieval centuries are fragmented on purpose in the sources: local houses, church land, caravan dues. Write them as a working political landscape, not as “dark ages.” Grade 10 Italians will walk into this already-named world.

cards.title: 6.3 Medieval Eritrea, 8th to 19th Century C.E
body: The decline of Aksum and the subsequent shift of political center to southern Abyssinia created a condition of relative autonomy in Eritrea.
With the gradual decline of the Aksumite Kingdom, a Kushitic people known as the Beja expanded and settled between Aswan in the Sudan and northwestern Eritrea beginning in the 8th century.
Through time, the area of Beja expansion came to include the whole coastal areas north of Hirghigo, Sahel, Barka and Anseba valley as well as most of the highlands.
The Bejas created five independent kingdoms, namely Naqis, Baqlin, Bazin, Jarin, and Qat'a.
The five kingdoms had different economic bases.

glossary.meaning: Eritrea is the first country in Africa to accept Islam.

tips.text: As part of the East African Great Rift Valley, in which most of the evidence for human origin has been discovered, Eritrea was inhabited by the first humans.
The discovery of a one-million year old hominid cranium in Buya, northern Danakil Depression, testifies to this fact.
For thousands of years Eritrea has been inhabited by hunter-gatherer communities.
Furthermore, it has a rich prehistory as shown by the sites found in places such as lower Barka valley, Aqordat, Qarora, Sellum Ba’atti, Zeban Ona Lebanos, Emba Foqada, and Asmara.
Generally speaking, present Eritrean society is the result of the interaction and integration of the indigenous communities with waves of incoming migrants.
There have been three main waves of migrations of different communities into Eritrea: the Nilotic, the Kushitic and Semitic.
By and large, Eritrean history can be classified into Ancient, Medieval and Modern periods.
Ancient Eritrean history goes back as far as the middle kingdom of Pharaonic Egypt. It stretches from 1500 B.C.E. to the seventh century C.E. It consists of pre-Aksumite and Aksumite periods.
Medieval Eritrean history extends from the decline of the Aksumite kingdom in the seventh century to the coming of the Italians in the last decade of the nineteenth century.
